paragraphs: The river rises in the hills above Thornwick and flows east for about 60 kilometres before it reaches the sea. Its valley is narrow in the upper reaches, where the river cuts through soft sandstone, and it widens near Marrowby.
Several mills were built along the river between 1780 and 1850. The mills used the river to turn their wheels, and the river carried their cloth to the coast on flat boats called keels.

sections.title: Wildlife
paragraphs: Otters returned to the river in 1998 after an absence of forty years. Salmon can be seen jumping at the weir in autumn, and herons nest in the tall alders along the banks.
Local volunteers count the birds every spring. In 2019 they recorded 64 species, including the kingfisher (a bright blue bird that dives for small fish) and the dipper, which walks underwater.
The water is clean enough for swimming in summer. Swimmers are asked to stay away from the weir and from the mill race, where the current is strong.
Fishing is allowed from March to October. Anglers need a permit, which costs 15 pounds for a season and can be bought at the post office in Thornwick.
